#Day4 | Advanced Course on MedTech Innovation, Intellectual Property & Patent Strategy | IIT Mandi Catalyst

IIT Mandi Catalyst continued Day 4 of the ongoing 5-Day Advanced Course on MedTech Innovation, Intellectual Property & Patent Strategy, being held from 12–16 October 2026.

💡 Session 5: From Patent Grant to Enforcement: Identifying Infringement and Protecting MedTech Innovations

The session was led by Mr. Naveen Mathur, Senior Patent Expert at Aksh IP Associates and Former Joint Controller of Patents & Designs, Indian Patent Office. The session explored comparative analysis of tube-securing devices, patent infringement assessment, Freedom to Operate (FTO), and the importance of documenting evidence to support patent enforcement and protect MedTech innovations.

💡 Session 6: Beyond Patent Filing: An Inventor’s Role in Patent Prosecution, FER Responses and Hearings

The session was led by Ms. Monika, Registered Patent Agent and Partner at Aksh IP Associates. Discussions covered patentability requirements, independent and dependent claims, addressing novelty objections, and drafting effective patent claims to strengthen patent applications and navigate the patent prosecution process.

🔹 Concluding Remarks: From Innovation to Incubation

At the conclusion of the day’s sessions, Prof. (Dr.) Dipankar Deb, Faculty In-Charge & Director – Incubation, IIT Mandi Catalyst, shared insights into the incubation journey and explained the significance of Technology Readiness Levels (TRL) and Business Readiness Levels (BRL) in assessing the technological maturity and commercial preparedness of innovations. Prof. (Dr.) Dipankar Deb highlighted how incubation support helps innovators refine their technologies, strengthen business models, and move towards successful commercialisation.

The sessions offered participants valuable insights into patent protection, prosecution, and the journey from MedTech research and innovation to incubation and market readiness.

Hitesh Shrimali | Ajoy Pathak | Sudeep Dey | Rishi S.

Last week, The Majurity TrustThe Majurity Trust  brought together a thoughtful room of impact-focused ecosystem leaders for a roundtable with Social AlphaSocial Alpha’s founder Manoj Kumar,Manoj Kumar,  during Singapore's busiest conference and F1 week.

One question framed the conversation: Who will do innovation for the underprivileged? And how do you actually create real impact while doing it?

Almost every big problem in this space, from irrigation for smallholder farmers to affordable diagnostics, has an element of market failure built into it. Writing a cheque is the simplest part. The real work is everything around it, which is why Social Alpha builds full-stack.

Labs, Ventures and Communities orbit around a single core: a de-risking engine.

A few lessons from a decade of doing this stood out from ManojManoj’s learning session:

1. This is not VC in the social sector, and it isn’t impact investing either. Social Alpha does invest, but the investment is philanthropic work. It carries a grant-like mindset, and equity is simply an instrument for sharing value.

2. The capital has to match the stage. Government and philanthropic capital are what carry a product through the valley of death. Commercial capital comes later, once there is a product and users (let's not call them customers), and not before.

3. Investors have to think like operators; until a venture can raise commercial money, it needs much more than funding. It needs lab access, space, partnerships, and hands-on support, more like a co-founder than a shareholder.

4. Start with the problem, and never lose sight of demand. Social Alpha works from problem statements and builds a thesis around each one. The question is always what innovation is needed and how people solve the problem today. And if you only start thinking about adoption once the innovation is ready, you’re already too late.

5. Some of the most useful learning has come from places nobody planned for, like discovering that farmers needed financing just to adopt the technology at all.

6. There was also a useful reminder for anyone raising philanthropic capital. Governments, corporates, foundations, family offices, and individual givers each define impact differently. Philanthropy needs market segmentation too.

A big thank you to Martin Tan and Jen Goh for hosting this robust roundtable and learning session.  Shaily Shah  Rehaa Malik

Taking Battery Innovation from the Lab to the Production Line

What does it take to turn a promising battery technology into a product that can be manufactured reliably at scale? The answer lies in the science, the engineering and the ability to solve the challenges that emerge along the way.

At Venture Center’s Energy Innovation Series, “Advanced Battery Innovation & Manufacturing: Insights from the UK Ecosystem,” Mr. Yahya Yahyavi Alvar, Head of Business Development, and Mr. John Poli, Manufacturing Operations Director, from the UK Battery Industrialisation Centre (UKBIC), shared perspectives from the UK’s battery manufacturing ecosystem.

Drawing on real-world customer examples, the speakers explored challenges ranging from electrode quality, coating defects and material elongation to cell design and battery module development. Their insights highlighted how process optimisation, simulation and industrial-scale trials help address manufacturing challenges that may not be apparent during laboratory development.

The central takeaway: developing a promising battery technology is only the beginning. Turning it into a commercially viable solution requires rigorous testing, manufacturing expertise and the ability to consistently reproduce results at scale.

Organised by the Centre of Excellence for Clean Energy and Green Hydrogen Innovations at Venture Center in collaboration with the Netzero Energy Transition Association (NETRA), and supported by Venture Center and MSInS, the session brought global manufacturing expertise into India’s battery innovation ecosystem. By connecting the UK’s experience in industrialising battery technologies with the challenges facing innovators today, it underscored the importance of bridging the gap between breakthrough research and manufacturing at scale.

As the innovation and research translation arm of Ahmedabad University, VentureStudio believes that meaningful ecosystem engagement is key to translating ideas and research into solutions that create real-world impact.
